The post Are technicians a hidden indicator of teaching excellence? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Tim Savage. Educational consultant at Tim Savage Consulting.

In my analysis of Teaching Excellence Framework (TEF) submissions, I found that between 2017 and 2023, the number of universities referencing technicians in their claims of teaching excellence increased from just under a fifth to a little over a third. Indeed, in 2023, 78 of 222 providers included technical staff in their narratives. Subsequently, I revisited the provider statements to ask a different question: is there an association between references to technicians in provider statements and the TEF ratings providers receive?

The pattern is striking: providers that referenced technicians were twice as likely to achieve an Overall Gold rating as those that did not. Furthermore, providers that did not reference technicians were more than three times as likely to receive Bronze or Requires Improvement.

While technicians are increasingly recognised for their contributions to learning and teaching, the association between their growing visibility within TEF and stronger institutional outcomes remains unexplored. In this blog, I consider why there seems to be such a strong connection between technicians and TEF performance.

Context

Higher education has evolved, and so has the workforce that enables it. Skills supply, employability and economic priorities have become increasingly prominent in higher-education policy, alongside a renewed emphasis on technical education. My doctoral research theorised a ‘technical turn’ in which contemporary technicians have moved from backstage roles concerned with maintaining and supporting equipment and facilities into more visible educational roles, teaching, and supporting learners to acquire and apply skills, and increasingly taking on duties previously deemed to be ‘academic’.

This shift is also evident in the sector’s language, structures and policy frameworks. HESA has recently developed more differentiated Professional, Technical and Operational Staff definitions to replace the generic and widely criticised ‘non-academic’ label. The Technician Commitment has helped advance the visibility, recognition, career development and sustainability of technical roles, while the Times Higher Education’s Outstanding Technician of the Year award offers a high-profile national platform for recognising technical contribution. In addition, REF 2029 will provide more explicit opportunities to represent technical contributions to research through the Strategy, People and Research Environment framework.

Despite these advances, technicians’ contribution to learning and teaching remains comparatively under-examined. The literature remains limited, with little consensus on what excellent technical teaching looks like, who should deliver it, or how to develop and integrate it. Addressing this is primarily an institutional responsibility, although sector bodies such as the QAA and Advance HE also have an important role in ensuring that quality and professional-development frameworks recognise the many technical colleagues who already teach and support the core curriculum. That gap is likely to become more urgent as universities prioritise technical expertise and skills teaching, with policy placing both at the centre of graduate outcomes and employability agendas.

Methodology and evidence

I reviewed all 222 TEF 2023 provider statements and compared institutional ratings according to whether technicians were referenced. Of the 78 providers that referenced technicians, 33.3% achieved Overall Gold, compared with 16.7% of the 144 that did not. Conversely, just 9.0% of technician-referencing providers received Bronze or Requires Improvement, compared with 30.6% of those making no reference to technicians.

The pattern was also apparent within the two TEF aspects. For Student Experience, 37.2% of technician-referencing providers achieved Gold, compared with 20.8% of those that did not. For Student Outcomes, just 10.3% received Bronze or Requires Improvement, compared with 29.2% of those where technicians were absent.

While variations exist beneath these headlines by institution type, discipline, scale and whether the provider is a Technician Commitment signatory and supports the pedagogic development of technical staff, including through Advance HE Fellowship, the same broad pattern persists: institutions in which technicians are visible, recognised and developed are associated with stronger TEF outcomes and much less likely to receive weaker ratings.

What might explain this?

One interpretation is that technicians themselves contribute directly to better learning and teaching. That is entirely plausible, but these data cannot establish causation.

Notably, higher-performing provider statements also tended to recognise other colleagues beyond academic teams, such as educational developers, librarians, careers professionals and learning-support staff. A broader interpretation is, therefore, that technician visibility may act as a measurable indicator of a more professionally inclusive, collaborative and integrated institutional culture.

Within high-performing institutions, responsibility for teaching quality and student experience appears less likely to sit within academic roles alone, and more likely to be understood as a shared institutional responsibility.

Lessons for future TEF

As the sector looks towards the next TEF, it does so with professional and support staff as the ‘invisible majority’, representing 56% of the workforce. The direction of travel in the Office for Students’ latest consultation outcome is therefore significant. Future TEF assessments will continue to assess course delivery, academic support, resources and student engagement, increasing the importance of understanding the wider systems, resources and staff through which students experience higher education. This direction is echoed in the QAA’s new Principle 3 guidance, which explicitly places staffing alongside physical and digital resources in delivering a high-quality learning experience.

For universities, while there may be a temptation to just ‘mention the technicians’, the challenge is much broader. Future TEF guidance should encourage providers to show how the knowledge and expertise of their entire workforce contributes to excellent student experiences and outcomes, while institutions themselves need to ensure that ‘one-university’ strategies are matched by cultures in which academic, technical and professional colleagues are recognised, connected and developed, and responsibility for teaching excellence is genuinely shared across the whole university.

title: A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know it | Gordon Brown

full_text:
We have not yet reached a 1968 moment, when students at the Sorbonne lit a fuse that detonated a crisis that eventually brought down the De Gaulle government. But in late 2026, starting with the symbolic act of young French people climbing the July Column at Paris’s Place de la Bastille, the world is experiencing the biggest outbreak of student demonstrations for 60 years.

When Italian students subsequently occupied a high school in Rome, they opened their demand for change with the words “like in France”. Youth demonstrations are now raging from India – where the government has responded with repressive force to the Cockroach movement – to Albania, where, after being out on the streets for nearly five months, students are demanding not only an end to corruption, but the replacement of the government.

But the most momentous set of protests has been in Serbia, where the Student List of candidates for national parliamentary elections has succeeded not just in dislodging a long-established, corruption-tainted government alleged to have links with organised crime, but in securing an electoral mandate. It is now poised to form a new administration. Nothing of this kind has ever happened before.

Student List is not only changing the political leadership of Serbia but popularising new methods of organising; it is building a system for selecting candidates from outside its own ranks, using methods such as open public assemblies with rotating delegates and specialised working groups. Eighty-five student assemblies selected the candidates, as an analysis of their internal rules explains. And the results are often surprising: the rector of Belgrade university, Vladan Djokić, was not selected as a candidate, despite being a longterm supporter of the movement and expected by many to play a major role in government.

Student List has been compared by the Croatian philosopher Srećko Horvat, who situates the movement within a longer tradition of direct democracy and collective self-organisation, to the Paris Commune of 1871. Its fundraising activites, however, are very much up to date: it reportedly crowdsourced almost €2m (£1.7m) from more than 26,000 individual donors during the election campaign.

The wave of youth protests comes after mobilisations in Kenya in 2024 and across Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines, Madagascar, Morocco and Peru in 2025. How far the Serbian grassroots model of organising will shape youth movements elsewhere remains to be seen. But according to Olivier Ertzscheid, a senior lecturer at the University of Nantes, “young people’s sense of belonging and social interaction is at play”, with social media now actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters – and driving momentum.

September and October have seen youth protests in Belgium, Austria, Greece and Italy over education funding; in Germany over the threat of compulsory military service; and in Spain and Portugal over the lack of affordable housing. But the protests have also spread well beyond Europe, to Indonesia, where youth demonstrations are focused on pollution; to Argentina over austerity; and to Chile and Colombia over funding cuts. Last weekend in Germany, a group called Gen Z regelt led demonstrations in 21 cities.

The protests will only intensify this month. In Australia, a big student demonstration is planned for 12 November, and student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a joint day of action protesting against the rising cost of education on 20 November.

Some years ago I wrote about a new generation of youth activists – of Bangladeshi schoolgirls campaigning against forced child marriage who had declared “child marriage-free zones”, and of Nigerian and other young people in Africa demanding their right to education. But the current youth rebellions are of a different order, breaking out in a new and more dangerous global environment and challenging authorities on issues well beyond education. Young people face an AI-led unemployment crisis; they lose out from the skewing of public spending towards older people, from restricted provision of education; they face a housing crisis and governments underplaying the importance of the climate emergency and intergenerational justice.

The youth jobs crisis will grow. The number of UK graduate jobs postings advertised on one big employment agency has declined from about 180,000 four years ago to 50,000 today. AI is thought to be a factor. Hi-tech employment of 18- to 24-year-olds declined by 30% between December 2019 and December 2025, whereas the sector itself expanded by 33% in that period. So as the government prepares to announce its review into youth employment, it is urgent we get nearly 1 million unemployed under-25s into work, giving priority to pre-apprenticeship training and restoring educational maintenance allowances, as well as radically reshaping a benefits system that is failing the younger generation.

But this is a worldwide problem. Because of ever-rising debt burdens and spiralling expenditures on defence and energy subsidies, governments are trapped in such a fiscal straitjacket that they will struggle to find the resources to meet young people’s aspirations. A large portion of public spending is captured by older generations, with schools and universities losing out as a result. Across the OECD, about half of health and social security spending goes to elderly people – those over 65 – despite them making up only 18.5% of the total population. In this tally, pensions are the biggest item, accounting for 38% of all social spending – but an understandably high portion of all health spending goes to older people, too. And with young people now taking home a far smaller share of income than earlier generations, income and wealth gaps between young and old have widened.

It’s time to join the dots. Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author of Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation, warns that the protests are morphing into a wider social movement. “There are inequalities at all levels,” she says, “with gaps widening between different social groups.” The triggers for the demonstrations vary from country to country, but the basic complaint is strikingly similar. Young people believe that any promises that they would do better than their parents’ generation have already been broken – and that case is a strong one. Liberal democracy itself is now on trial.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010, and is United Nations special envoy for global education

This article was amended on 3 November 2026. An earlier version stated a student demonstration in Australia was planned for 11 November. The date of the protest was changed to 12 November.

full_text:
SARATOGA SPRINGS, N.Y. — “Overwhelming.”

That’s how 17-year-old high school senior Alex Zaret described the college admissions process during a tour this fall of Skidmore College — the fourth campus Zaret had visited, with another half a dozen to go.

“It is kind of a full-time job,” Zaret’s father, Owen, said.

He wasn’t joking. With research to do, visits to make and applications and financial forms to fill out, “it’s a lot, and it’s a lot on top of two full-time-employed parents and a very engaged high school student,” Owen Zaret said.

But even in the year or so that the family has been doing this, the Zarets have detected a subtle shift.

“It used to be more an ivory tower approach,” Zaret said, which signaled, “ ‘You’re lucky if you come here.’ And now, I think, for a variety of reasons, that’s changed. It’s more like, ‘We want you to be here.’ ”

As they compete to attract a dwindling supply of students, colleges are striving to transform an admissions process that has often been intimidating, secretive and stressful into an experience that’s open, easier and downright friendly.

“It’s one of those things that’s in everybody’s interest,” said Marc Conner, the president of Skidmore, which has been making a particular push to do this. After all, he said, “we depend on students coming to our campuses and, when they do come, getting them to enroll.”

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Some universities and colleges are waiving application fees and promising additional financial aid for students who show up for campus tours. Public universities in 17 states now admit high school students who haven’t even applied, according to the Education Commission of the States; more than 150 private colleges also make direct admissions offers to students who fill out the Common App, a standardized online application used by about 1,200 institutions. And the overall odds of getting accepted to college are going up.

Now Skidmore and a small number of other institutions have taken a surprising next step. They’re enlisting faculty to help recruit new students by meeting with and opening their labs and classrooms to prospective and admitted applicants — a role previously left to the admissions office.

“It creates a feeling of what it would be like to be seen, valued and to find a place of belonging on a campus,” said Jess Ricker, the college’s vice president for enrollment. And that, Ricker said, can help distinguish Skidmore from the other schools on students’ lists.

Admissions leaders are looking for any advantage. Two-thirds of them had trouble meeting their enrollment targets in at least one of the last two years, according to a survey by the ratings platform Niche. Ninety-seven percent expect the competition to increase even more.

The problem is that the supply of traditional-age freshmen has begun to fall, with the number of high school graduates nationwide projected to decline by 13 percent between last year and 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. The proportion of high school graduates choosing to go on to college right away is also down, from 70 percent in 2016 to 63 percent in 2024, the most recent year for which the figure is available, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports.

Related: Colleges ease the dreaded admissions process as the supply of applicants declines

One little-noticed result: Being accepted to college now is generally easier than in the past — and easier than Americans seem to think it is.

The average overall undergraduate acceptance rate for first-time applicants is nearly 80 percent at public and 70 percent at private, nonprofit colleges and universities, the National Association for College Admission Counseling, or NACAC, reports. That’s up from 68 percent and 65 percent, respectively, about 10 years ago. Nearly 9 in 10 private, nonprofit four-year universities and colleges admit half or more of applicants, according to separate research by the conservative think tank the American Enterprise Institute — a proportion that is also up over the last decade.

This news has been slow to trickle down to students. More than 40 percent of 18- to 29-year-olds wrongly think it’s harder for today’s students to get into college than it was for people in their parents’ generation, a Pew Research Center survey found.

“Most of the public actually doesn’t understand that the majority of institutions in the United States actually accept the majority of students who apply,” said Angel Pérez, NACAC’s CEO.

He blamed an obsession with impossible-seeming acceptance rates at institutions such as the California Institute of Technology, Harvard, Princeton and Stanford, which each take about one applicant in 25.

“If you looked at mainstream media stories, you would automatically assume if you were a high school student or a parent, ‘It’s so hard to get into college,’ or, ‘I’m never going to get in,’ ” Pérez said.

In fact, only 33 colleges and universities in the country admit 10 percent or fewer of their undergraduate applicants, NACAC figures show.

Related: College admissions offices take on a new role: Coaxing accepted students to show up

The intensifying competition for them might be good for students, but it’s making life tougher for many colleges. At many, offices of admission are struggling to shake what Ricker joked is their historic reputation as uncaring “offices of rejection.”

That’s among the reasons some are starting to appeal to the faculty for help. At Ohio Northern University, at least one member of the faculty now meets with every visiting applicant. Faculty at Washington College in Maryland sit down with visiting applicants on designated Fridays during the admissions season and at open houses.

“We’re seeing more colleges leaning into more engagement involving everyone on the campus,” said Rob Springall, a consultant at the executive search firm WittKieffer and former executive director of undergraduate admissions at Pennsylvania State University. “Presidents and vice presidents of enrollment are telling people that every interaction counts.”

There’s another reason for this push that’s less widely understood among consumers. As students hedge their bets by applying to more colleges than their historical counterparts did — Common App users now apply to an average of more than seven schools apiece, a number that’s been steadily increasing — it’s getting harder for enrollment managers to predict how many of the students they admit will actually enroll. In admissions lingo, this is called the yield, and nearly 8 in 10 enrollment leaders in that Niche survey said it’s become another on their growing list of problems.

Yield declined from 32 percent to 22 percent at public colleges and universities and from 24 percent to 18 percent at private nonprofits, on average, between 2014 and 2024, federal data shows. That’s the last period for which the figures are available.

This means colleges have to admit around five times as many students as they hope to enroll — and that campus hospitality can’t end with the admissions deadline. Admitted applicants need to be persuaded to follow through and put down their deposits, including the many who come back to take another look around.

Colleges “are realizing that everyone has to help with the recruiting process, full force,” said Leah Beth Hubbard, assistant vice president of enrollment strategies at the enrollment consulting firm The Parish Group. She advises clients to “teach everyone to smile. Teach everyone to introduce themselves and say what they do at the institution.”

Related: A trend colleges might not want applicants to notice: It’s becoming easier to get in

Coaxing faculty to do this, on top of their existing obligations, isn’t always easy, campus leaders said — at least, at first.

“Some faculty didn’t want to be part of it,” said Johnnie Johnson, Washington College’s vice president for enrollment management. “They’d say, ‘You go recruit and I’ll teach.’ ”

Like other university and college administrators, Johnson said he countered with a frank assessment of enrollment trends.

“When you put a financial figure on every student who comes in, that equates to programmatic funding. That equates to raises,” he said. And faculty are seeing what happens when those numbers fall. “They have colleagues who have been at colleges that closed” or whose programs have been cut, said Johnson. “They don’t want to be next.”

Now, he said, “We have faculty volunteering” to let applicants sit in on their classes. “We have faculty volunteering to send emails. When we do our open houses, the faculty who might not have participated in those are more willing to participate.”

Skidmore, which has about 2,700 students on a pastoral campus near the famous Saratoga Race Course, hasn’t experienced the problems many other small private, nonprofit colleges are confronting. It’s in the enviable position of seeing its number of applications rise, not fall; unlike many other colleges, its acceptance rate is down, from 37 percent 10 years ago to 24 percent today. Yield is up slightly, to an above-average 24 percent.

Still, said Conner, the president, “the challenges are real. And even if the school is doing all right during these times, we’re still facing the same headwinds as everybody else. So you’d better pay attention to it, or you’re going to be in trouble pretty soon.”

As elsewhere, part of the response has been to make prospective applicants and their families feel more a part of the campus when they visit, rather than spectators disconnected from it. Everyone from dining hall workers to groundskeepers is encouraged to be welcoming, and faculty are urged to meet with students and let them sit in on classes and in labs.

Related: Experts say higher education is an industry in turmoil. The collateral damage is widespread

“I can’t think of a professor who [said], ‘Don’t bother me with that. That’s not my thing,’ ” said Conner. “It helps that we’re in a tough time in higher ed and they see what’s happening at other schools, and they know a school is going to rise or fall depending on how much the community joins together.”

More than three-quarters of admitted students who came to the campus last year other than for a weekend open house requested to sit in on a class or meet with a faculty member, the college says. That added up to 300 face-to-face visits.

There’s not yet data about whether those young visitors apply or enroll. But psychology department chair Becca Johnson, who often meets with applicants, said she hears feedback that the extra effort makes a difference.

One mother told her, “ ‘You know, my student has applied to so many schools, been accepted, had a number of wonderful possible possibilities,’ ” Johnson recounted. “ ‘And you’re the first person from outside of an admissions office to contact us.’ And that was so meaningful for them in their decision.”

Johnson, whose students call her Dr. J, displays an award in her office for her work with the admissions office. She keeps emails from students who followed up to thank her or let her know that they were planning to enroll.

“Students and parents, they’re savvy shoppers. They’re making really wise decisions,” said Johnson, the mother of a college student herself. “And I think more information is better than less.”

title: Academic Freedom Protects Politics
summary:
Academic Freedom Protects Politics
Sara Brady Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

Attempts to suppress “political” ideas have no place in a free country or a free university.

Byline(s)
John K. Wilson
full_text:
With the midterm elections being held tomorrow, the usual moans and cries are heard about how professors shouldn’t be political. The American Association of University Professors has come under fire for endorsing political candidates in this election for the first time in its century-long existence.

It’s hard to understand why political positions should offend anyone. Everyone who votes has a political preference, and it’s common for unions to endorse political candidates. No one doubts that some political candidates support higher education and free speech on campus and some candidates attack academic freedom. The AAUP certainly should speak out against legislation that endangers their core values of academic freedom. Why shouldn’t the AAUP also speak out against the politicians who vote for and implement the laws that violate academic freedom?

Anyone who thinks that political endorsements endanger the AAUP’s commitment to its principles is mistaken; political endorsements are the effective expression of the AAUP’s commitment to these principles.

Some members might be offended by the AAUP’s stand. But many more members would be offended if the AAUP failed to take a stand for academic freedom. Indifference and silence in the face of the worst attack against academic freedom in American history is just as much of a political position as taking a public stand—it’s simply a worse political position.

What’s most alarming to me about the attacks on the AAUP is how they reflect a misguided belief that political ideas are not protected by academic freedom. Tammi Rossman-Benjamin, director of the AMCHA Initiative, wrote an Oct. 29 op-ed for the Washington Times denouncing the AAUP’s endorsements and asserting that “Academic freedom was meant to protect scholarship from politics. Instead, some of the nation’s most prominent academic organizations are invoking the phrase to shield their own political activism.”

Rossman-Benjamin is completely wrong. Academic freedom protects scholarship from politics by defending the right of academics to express political ideas.

Incredibly, Rossman-Benjamin attacks the Middle East Studies Association for its Oct. 8 report “Lessons in Repression” because it “documents nearly 200 incidents of alleged retaliation against university employees for pro-Palestinian speech and activism, mostly outside the classroom.”

Rossman-Benjamin wonders, “How did an organization established to promote Middle East scholarship make defending political activism a major institutional project?” That’s easy to answer: because scholars have been attacked for their political views. In order to protect scholarship, you have to protect the right for scholars to express their political ideas without retaliation.

There is no “political activism” exception to academic freedom. In fact, the reverse is true: The primary purpose of academic freedom is to defend the rights of professors accused of expressing political views unpopular with those in power.

The origins of academic freedom in America are based upon freedom for political activism.

In 1894, the University of Wisconsin issued the first institutional statement in defense of academic freedom, proclaiming that it could not punish or even criticize Richard Ely for his political views supporting the labor movement and teaching about socialism. But few universities, then or since, have embraced this fundamental value.

In 1895, the University of Chicago fired Edward Bemis after he publicly criticized railroad owners. In 1900, Stanford University fired Edward Ross for his economic views. In 1915, Scott Nearing was fired by the University of Pennsylvania for his opposition to child labor. All of these cases helped influence the formation of the AAUP and its 1915 Declaration of Principles in defense of a new American conception of academic freedom that went beyond teaching and research to include the right to express extramural utterances, by which it meant controversial political views.

The attack on political activism—coming from politicians, administrators and commentators alike—is an attack on academic freedom, intellectual diversity and institutional neutrality.

The Trump administration’s Compact 2.0 letter on Aug. 3 to all colleges demanded answers about how they are suppressing “political” scholarship: “Some academic disciplines and departments have subordinated the scholarly pursuit to political and social goals, as documented in the recent Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences. When disciplines skew toward one side of the ideological spectrum, the truth-seeking function of the university suffers and public trust declines. How will your institution encourage intellectual pluralism in all its academic units? How will your faculty hiring and evaluation practices support academic vitality and ensure that all relevant perspectives are taken seriously? And how will your school ensure the research enterprise is dedicated to advancing knowledge, deepening understanding, and serving the American people who fund it?”

Every university must encourage intellectual pluralism, academic vitality and the advancement of knowledge by firmly rejecting the dictates of the Department of Education’s repressive query. Political and social goals are not the subordination of scholarly pursuit, but an entirely proper form of scholarship. The government is prohibited by the First Amendment from suppressing “political and social goals,” and universities are prohibited from similar repression by standards of academic freedom and institutional neutrality, which prohibits administrators from deciding that some scholars’ views are deemed to have the wrong political and social goals.

If you believe that some people have the wrong political views or bring those ideas into inappropriate contexts, then you are perfectly free to criticize them. But it’s time to recognize that the attempt to suppress “political” ideas has no place in a free country or a free university.

title: Focus, and Clarity of Mission
summary:
Focus, and Clarity of Mission
Sara Brady Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

It can be frustrating to read press accounts of higher education that generalize entirely from high-profile, elite universities.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
An exchange a few days ago got me reflecting on what makes community colleges different from the rest of higher education.

It’s a young sector—half of the community colleges in the U.S. were founded in the 1960s. (My own, Westmoreland, was founded in 1970.) Most started small, and most served primarily the lower-income side of the student population. Taken together, those factors mean that most community colleges don’t have significant endowments, if they have one at all. The wonders of compound growth haven’t had time to happen, and the number of alums who’ve reached the pinnacle of their earning years is still relatively small.

That has consequences for the business model. The Truman Commission (1947–48) recommended that a national network of community colleges would be free; in most of the country, that didn’t happen, and in the places where it did (CUNY, California), “free” fell victim to budget crunches in the 1970s. Over time, in most places, tuition has covered an ever-greater share of costs, even though the colleges weren’t built for that.

Governance models tend to be complicated, though this varies by state. In some states, the boards are constituted by the various high schools in the colleges service area. (There, community colleges have superintendents and districts, much like K–12.) In others, boundaries are defined by county lines, with varying roles for state-level intervention; in still others, counties don’t matter at all. Community colleges are often seen as arms of local workforce development, adding a new set of stakeholders. And funding streams vary from “millages” to state and/or local appropriations, though again, those have lagged.

But the single biggest difference, to my mind, is focus.

Most community colleges don’t have dorms, or if they do, they serve a relatively small portion of the student body. Athletics tend to be low-profile and tend to favor lower-cost sports. (Football exists in the community college world, but it’s the exception. Basketball is much more common. I’ve never worked at a community college that had football, but they’ve all had basketball.) It’s rare to see more than a handful of students watching a game, even when there’s no charge for tickets. Student life activities exist, but they’re less expansive than you’d find at a residential four-year campus.

Universities teach, and perform research, and support high-profile sports, and provide “the college experience.” Community colleges teach. They focus on one thing.

That’s evolving, of course. Over the past few years, I’ve seen them become more active as conveners of local employers, and as workforce training providers. They can play the role of Switzerland in local turf battles, which is more useful than many people realize. Teaching, in this context, covers both credit and noncredit instruction. Our EMT training doesn’t offer academic credit, but it’s crucial for the local community.

In the new focus on workforce, I sometimes worry that the historic transfer mission gets a bit lost. Transfer remains a crucial on-ramp to higher degrees and higher-paying careers for students who might be place-bound for economic or familial reasons. It also offers a second chance for late-blooming students whose high school transcripts may be a bit uneven. This is the “college” part of “community college,” and it’s worth keeping.

In my (mumble, cough) years of community college administration across several states, I’ve never heard anyone say that we should take it easy on a student because he’s a star athlete. It has never happened. I doubt that it ever will. That’s not where our priorities are.

It can be frustrating to read press accounts of higher education that generalize entirely from high-profile, elite universities. From The New York Times, for instance, you’d think that faculty political leanings, activist students and nearly six-figure cost of attendance were the main issues facing higher education. Here, they simply aren’t. And with over a thousand community colleges across the country, I don’t think that counts as special pleading. More students attend community colleges than the entire Ivy League combined.

For all (money) of the frustrations (money) of the sector (money), one thing it absolutely has is clarity of mission. It has focus. It would be nice if the sector drew a bit more attention.

title: What Will Become of America’s Research Institutions?
summary:
What Will Become of America’s Research Institutions?
Susan H. Greenberg Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

Drawing on his new book, former Boston University President Robert Brown discusses the evolving role of universities in the U.S. research enterprise.

Byline(s)
Susan H. Greenberg
full_text:
Robert Brown has spent his career at research universities, first as professor of chemical engineering and provost at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and now as president emeritus of Boston University, where he held the top post from 2005 to 2023, presiding over BU’s 2012 acceptance into the Association of American Universities. His new book, Fighting Fires and Building Flywheels: How We Sustain America’s Research Universities (The MIT Press), blends history, memoir and analysis to provide a nuanced picture of what it takes to build and operate research universities—the flywheels—as well as the unpredictable crises that regularly erupt to test them.

He spoke with Inside Higher Ed via Zoom about how research institutions have evolved, why they remain vital and just how much damage the second Trump administration has done to the whole enterprise. Excerpts of the conversation follow, edited for length and clarity.

Q: When you first got to BU in 2005, you told everybody you wanted to make it a “great urban research university.” What did you mean by that?

A: One thing that’s important about Boston University—and most universities—is they operate in some kind of regional or community environment. I’d been at MIT for 25 years, and what I realized pretty quickly is that though I’d just moved across the [Charles] River—I could literally see MIT from where I was sitting—the move was profoundly different because MIT is a national global resource that Cambridge interfaces with, while Boston University is really integral to the fabric of Boston. We are this hybrid of a research university that attracts students from all over the world, but we also are very much integral to the environment. And I think that’s true of every major research university: At some level, they’re responsible to the community.

Q: You took the helm at BU following a long, tumultuous presidency by John Silber. How did you know that BU had the potential to become a great research university?

A: I did my due diligence before I took the job. I knew the pockets of where we had really good faculty, and where we had really underresourced but quality research efforts. So I thought the underpinnings were there, and it was going to take a while to get it together and get a system where it was seen by the outside world. Plus, I knew the AAU well from my time at MIT.

Q: How did your leadership style differ from Silber’s, whom you call “autocratic” in the book?

A: Over the last few decades, leadership at most research universities has become too diffuse; schools and colleges are independent. What that does is make it pretty much an oxymoron that the university has a strategy, because the strategy is a collection of what each of the schools and colleges wanted to do.

Successful research universities need to have strong central leadership. John believed that, too, but he did too many things that weren’t focused on the university. He ran for governor. If you were a corporate board and your CEO ran for major public office, would you believe he should be your CEO?

I’m a strategic pragmatist. I love building things, but I can only do it if I have the money to do it. I’m not going to risk the institution and its mission for the glory of the institution. I’m pragmatic about the resources we have and making sure we use them to serve our mission well. And I think a lot about the longer-term strategy of the institution, to fulfill the view that it’s going to be here for a long time.

Q: You note that research universities had troubles long before Trump started slashing funding in 2025. Can you talk about that?

A: Going back to even before the [2008] financial crisis, but clearly by 2010, the research university system in this country was showing wear and tear—for two reasons, and then a third was added. The first was the federal government’s expenditures on research have not kept up with inflation, or with how many institutions want to be research universities. And even though the universities spend money on research, they are not profit centers. The amount of money they spend has been going up and up over the last several decades, even before Trump. I always use 2022 data as my benchmark: R-1 universities in this country were spending 45 cents for every federal dollar they got, according to their own reported data to the National Science Foundation. And that number had been climbing.

At the same time, starting after the financial crisis, the value proposition question in the public was exploding. People were saying, “Why does it cost so much to get a degree? What’s the value of the degree?” That drumbeat has just accelerated.

There was a disconnect; ACE [the American Council on Education], which now runs the Carnegie Classification, was exploding the number of institutions called R-1s. You see it in their advertising, these institutions crowing about how they got R-1 status, right? I have data that shows that some of those that are growing are spending enormous amounts of their own money on research.

Then Trump basically took a sledgehammer to the cracks and blew the system apart by making it even harder to get research money and launching what I would call an outright attack against the private research university sector—especially in the Northeast. When the house was already burning, he started a big dumpster fire in the front yard.

The third thing that people didn’t see coming was the demographic cliff—major flagship universities missing their enrollment targets and cutting their budgets. And then Trump, of course, adds in, “Well, we’re not going to have any foreign students.” Just to make things worse.

Q: On top of that, supporting research traditionally has been a bipartisan enterprise, but now it’s become so politicized.

A: The Vannevar Bush Covenant [establishing the postwar government-university research partnership] held literally from the ’50s through the ’80s into the ’90s, right? But by the financial crisis … Look at the NSF budget for the last 15 years. That bipartisan group, although they would say they supported research, wouldn’t spend more money. It wasn’t a priority. Even the Chinese expenditures, which are just amazingly large, didn’t move them to action.

I mean, it wasn’t hostile like it is now. But if you look at the budgets that were passed, there were things not funded. A great example was the CHIPS Act, and that was under Biden. Everyone agreed that we needed to renew the semiconductor industry in this country. They passed the CHIPS Act but appropriated no money for it. And then they’re surprised nothing happened.

Q: Do you think the shift in public attitudes about cost and ROI played a role in the reluctance to fund?

A: It all stirs together. We didn’t do a good job, really, talking about how this country has moved to where the research universities are doing a huge fraction of the basic research, which is very different than in the ’50s and ’60s. The corporate laboratories that used to exist are almost nonexistent today. And we didn’t make the case to the public in a way they would believe that this longer-term view of research was important.

It was interesting looking at public data during COVID, because there was a blip up. When the vaccines hit, public sentiment went up. But the blip didn’t last.

A lot of university leaders go around saying, “We just have to tell the story better.” But we’ve been saying that for like 25 years; it’s a trite thing to say. Telling the story better is not going to fix the system.

Q: Do you think there are too many research universities?

A: I actually think that’s not the way to think about it—prescribe a number in a free-market enterprise? It’s just not the American way. The better way of thinking about it is institutions that cannot be everything to everybody have to decide where they’re going to be known and pick those areas where they can build faculties and be nationally competitive. It may be in philosophy, or foreign language, or quantum physics. But very few universities today can afford to do everything well, and yet they try, and that’s what spreads the money out and makes the enterprise so expensive.

You see this in the privates. You also see it in the publics—not so much the big flagship publics, which sort of have a mandate to be a full, comprehensive university—but the others do not have that mandate. They just take that mandate.

Q: So what’s the solution?

A: Two things are going to have to happen. One is the university is going to have to learn how to focus and thrive in a world that has less resources than they think they can get. They’re going to have to rethink the balance of their educational mission and research.

And at the same time, we’ve got to figure out a way to reinvent the covenant with the federal government, so that there’s more predictability in what’s going to happen. Right now, the amount of uncertainty is just appalling.

Q: That seems easier said than done at the moment.

A: At the end of the day, if we got back to where we were at the beginning of the Trump administration, we were still in trouble. We still didn’t have enough money. And now there’s so much smoke from the turmoil that the administration’s created that it allows universities to divert all their attention to that. There’s a whole group of leaders and institutions that are just fighting the dumpster fire, believing that once that’s out, everything will be fine. It wasn’t fine to begin with.

One of the biggest challenges we have is the decreasing amount of time university leaders stay in their positions. Because these are not short-term problems. A couple of years ago, a group of new presidents asked me for my advice for success. My answer was, “Stay a while.” If I had left after five years, nothing would have happened.

Q: Is there a viable funding alternative to the federal government–university model?

A: I don’t think so. People always talk about philanthropic and corporate funding. But if you look at all the research universities in the country, corporate funding is like 4.5 percent of their total funding, right? So if it doubled, it’s 10 percent, compared to the federal government’s 55 percent. The same thing for foundations. And the other thing about foundations and corporate funding is it is not spread evenly. If I’m a corporation today and I have an area I want to support, I go find the best people on the planet—I don’t care where they are—and I fund them.

Q: Is there a post–research university world where something different moves in to fill that space?

A: The interesting thing is if you started a university with a clean piece of paper today, would it look the way we look? The answer is no. Some of my friends at Carnegie Mellon are going to do that in Miami. My understanding is that they’re not going to try to recreate CMU in Miami; it’ll be much more focused and integrated than the Pittsburgh campus.

Can you do that with an existing university? It’s very hard to carve a space out for a new discipline or something that’s truly interdisciplinary in a university that has strong departments. We create more disciplines as we go, and the university gets increasingly fractionated. Most of the problems that are interesting that we work on do not have disciplinary boundaries, yet our universities still do.

At the same time, knowledge is becoming more ubiquitous. I mean, I can get knowledge today off the internet or with my friend Claude at a rate that was unimaginable when I was a student, and I can get knowledge about anything.

I am a big proponent of tenure; I don’t see a way around tenure. The challenge is that your faculty turns over so slowly, which is an issue with AI because that slow turnover is going to make adoption of new pedagogy very difficult. I don’t have any idea how that’s going to work.

title: Ahead of Midterms, Faculty Report Self-Censoring on DEI, Politics
summary:
Ahead of Midterms, Faculty Report Self-Censoring on DEI, Politics
Emma Whitford Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

Also in Inside Higher Ed’s latest faculty survey, professors report that AI has eroded their confidence in the authenticity of students’ work and damaged trust.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
Six in 10 faculty members told Inside Higher Ed in a new survey that their enthusiasm for working in higher education has somewhat or significantly declined over the past two years. Headlines since 2024 offer plenty of possible explanations for their growing fatigue: The federal government has slashed research budgets and politicians have painted professors as boogeymen. State legislatures are exerting increasing control over how and what faculty discuss in the classroom, and even tenured professors have lost their jobs over social media posts. Artificial intelligence, now ubiquitous, has touched nearly every part of professors’ jobs, from teaching and grading to research and publishing.

Ahead of tomorrow’s midterm elections, Inside Higher Ed and Hanover Research asked 1,665 faculty members how their jobs have changed since 2024, including whether they’re self-censoring on hot-button issues and if they’d like to stay or leave their current state. The survey also asked about the impact AI has had on their relationships with students.

Hundreds of respondents reported all kinds of self-censorship. Nearly half—47 percent—of faculty members said that they’re refraining from making extramural utterances, such as posting on Facebook, because of the situation on their campus or the political environment at large. Another 43 percent reported that they’re refraining from communicating with students about certain topics in and out of class, and 24 percent said they’re holding back from researching or publishing about certain topics they would otherwise pursue. The results on all of these questions were similar for tenured, tenure-track and non-tenure-track faculty members.

Four in 10 faculty members said they’re refraining from including certain materials on their syllabus that they would otherwise include. Syllabi have been increasingly scrutinized by Republican politicians, and some faculty members have been subject to doxing in recent years because of what’s listed in their course materials. A growing number of states, including Alabama, Florida, North Carolina and Texas, now require professors to post their syllabi publicly.

Asked about which topics are chilled, 50 percent of faculty respondents said they feel less free to discuss diversity, equity and inclusion than they did a year ago. That’s a decrease from the 65 percent of faculty respondents who said the same in 2024, but DEI is still the No. 1 topic for self-censoring. Black and Hispanic respondents were more likely than the group over all to report self-censoring over DEI, with 69 percent and 55 percent, respectively, reporting they felt less free to discuss the topic than they were a year ago.

Forty-five percent of respondents said they feel less free to discuss the Israeli/Palestinian conflict than they did a year ago, and 44 percent said they feel less free to talk about federal politics.

Some 45 percent of faculty members also pointed to federal interference in higher education as one of the things that concerns them most about the state of higher ed today, ahead of issues such as declining enrollment (which 16 percent cited as a top concern), the cost of college (24 percent), declining academic freedom (22 percent) and state-level interference in higher ed (20 percent). Notably, none of the respondents said they had no concerns about the state of higher education.

Over a quarter of respondents said they feel less free to discuss Charlie Kirk—not surprising given that dozens of professors and staff members were fired or disciplined for posting on social media about Kirk in the wake of his death in September 2025.

“I am not surprised that these are the topics faculty avoid the most, especially since we have seen many high-profile cases of faculty being punished or fired for discussing them,” said Kristina Brezicha, an associate professor of educational leadership at Neumann University who studies education and democracy. “On DEI and Palestine, faculty have been fired or disciplined for their speech or actions on and off campus.”

In a polarized era of social media and secret recordings, she continued, federal politics is another area where “many faculty members fear retribution for their statements.”

Faculty members were least likely to report self-censoring about contraception, with only 11 percent feeling less free to discuss the topic, compared with 23 percent who said the same in 2024. Talk about vaccines also appears to be less of a concern, with only 18 percent of faculty reporting they feel less free to discuss them than they did a year ago, compared with 26 percent who said the same in 2024.

Regarding their general enthusiasm about working in higher ed now versus two years ago, nearly two in three tenured or tenure-track faculty say it’s decreased somewhat (37 percent) or significantly (26 percent). Among part-time, non-tenure-track faculty, 37 percent say it’s decreased somewhat, and 14 percent, significantly. For full-time, non-tenure-track faculty, the numbers are 41 percent and 20 percent, respectively. Relatively few respondents overall say their enthusiasm has increased somewhat or significantly in the last two years (9 percent combined).

Would They Stay or Would They Go?

Asked whether they would—if they could—leave the state where their institution is located because of the broader political environment, about a quarter of faculty said yes. Their answers varied by region: Just 2 percent of faculty in New England said they would leave if they could, while 39 percent of faculty in Plains states (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) and 37 percent of faculty in the Southeast (Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia) said they would leave the state if they could. In Texas specifically (n=131), 58 percent of faculty reported wanting to leave the state, as did 49 percent of faculty in Florida (n=49).

State political climates are “likely also influencing where faculty apply for jobs,” Brezicha said. “When I worked in Georgia, job candidates asked about the political environment out of concern for their ability to conduct research, but also, more broadly, for their ability to thrive in a state with these types of repressive laws.”

Though they may want to leave, other surveys show that professors aren’t actually moving out of their states at such high rates. Inside Higher Ed asked the faculty members who would like to leave or who aren’t sure about leaving (n=583) what’s stopping them, and many cited having children or other family established in their state (42 percent) as a significant barrier. Other barriers included difficulty finding comparable employment elsewhere (42 percent) and fondness for their job or institution, despite the broader political climate (40 percent). About three in 10 professors said their spouse’s job was a deterrent to leaving, and about a quarter were concerned about losing salary.

In Inside Higher Ed’s recent survey of provosts with Hanover, academic leaders reported that overall faculty turnover had cooled since 2024, the end of the Great Resignation.

As for how the upcoming midterms might impact their institution’s ability to deliver on its mission, some 32 percent of professors said they believe the results will have a somewhat or very positive impact. That’s roughly double the share who believe it will have any kind of negative impact (17 percent). The remainder—51 percent—don’t expect any impact. Self-identified Democrats in the sample (n=843) are more likely than the group as a whole to expect a positive effect, at 40 percent. Among Republicans (n=91), it’s 10 percent; most of these respondents expect the effect to be neutral (74 percent).

AI Has Damaged Trust in Students

Despite faculty worries about state-level politics and federal interference in higher education, the thing that concerned faculty respondents most about the state of higher education today was the increased use of generative and agentic AI. Half of faculty members reported that this was a top concern.

Nearly nine in 10 of faculty respondents said AI has had a somewhat or very negative impact on their confidence in the authenticity of students’ work or communications. Social sciences (90 percent) and arts and humanities faculty (92 percent) were more likely to say this than STEM professors (86 percent) and those in law or business (82 percent), but sentiment skews negative regardless of field. About two-thirds of all faculty respondents (67 percent) said AI has had a somewhat or very negative impact on trust between them and their students.

The survey figures “echo what we’ve been seeing and hearing from people everywhere,” said Paul LeBlanc, former president of Southern New Hampshire University and author of the book Reclaiming Purpose: The University in an AI World.

“Faculty of all stripes are seeing students use AI in ways that undermine the learning process and also the trust in the work,” said José Antonio Bowen, a senior fellow at the American Association of Colleges and Universities. “Faculty mostly like students and we want them to succeed, and I think a lot of faculty realize that if you give out candy, people are going to take it, even when they know it is bad for you.”

The reported negative effects of AI have yet to significantly sour professor-student relationships altogether, the data shows. More than half (53 percent) of faculty respondents said AI has had no effect on their overall relationships with students, while 40 percent said it’s had a somewhat or very negative effect, and 7 percent said it’s had a somewhat or extremely positive effect.

“That’s a testimony to faculty’s ability to separate these two things out. In other words, ‘I’m not trusting what I’m seeing in the work that my students are submitting, but I still love my students. That’s only one piece of my relationship with them,’” LeBlanc said. “It’s a reassuring and positive thing to see that.”

Faculty members were most positive about AI when it came to their ability to provide students with timely or individualized support. Nearly one in five respondents (18 percent) said AI has had an extremely or somewhat positive impact on their ability to do so, while most faculty—65 percent—said it has had no effect.

“So few professors report positive impacts from AI, but why would they? I don’t think we are deploying AI in our teaching and learning, generally speaking, in ways that build relationships,” LeBlanc said. For example, instead of going to office hours to ask their professor a question, students can now just ask an AI chatbot, he said.

“When you go to the office to ask your [professor] something, you might get your particular question answered, but it’s also a chance to get to know each other,” he said. “It’s a chance to connect.”

title: Colleges Prepare for Credit Transfer Regulations
summary:
Colleges Prepare for Credit Transfer Regulations
jessica.blake@… Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:00 AM

While some colleges are already working to improve transfer policies and accepting more credits, Trump’s new standards likely will accelerate reforms.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
When Stephen Pruitt, president of one of the nation’s largest accreditors, started to develop a voluntary program designed to improve the portability of institutions’ general education credits, he hoped that just 50 of his member institutions would express interest. But now, as the agency’s Transfer Credit Consortium prepares to convene for its first meeting, more than 230 of the agency’s roughly 800 institutions are on board.

“I think we had 100 institutions within six days of announcing the consortium,” said Pruitt who leads the Commission on Colleges and Universities, formerly known as the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges. “It was gangbusters. And so much so that my assistant and I had a hard time keeping up with the number of emails that were coming in saying, ‘Count us in. We want to be a part of this.’”

In November, a panel of faculty members representing the interested institutions will decide what it takes to be a member of the consortium. For example, it’s undecided whether colleges will have to accept 100 percent of one another’s gen ed credits, or if they can make exceptions for specific courses like introductory math in an engineering major. But once that framework is decided, there will be a standard set of course equivalencies applied universally across the institutions that opt in. That way, students who transfer among those institutions have clear, common pathways they can rely on, without losing copious credits, time and money.

The goal is to have the consortium’s policies established by May. “Then we can start finding out who’s really willing to put some of this skin in the game,” Pruitt said.

The Trump administration, however, has made clear that even if CCU and other accreditors use voluntary programs like the consortium for now, they will eventually have to set stricter mandatory standards to improve their colleges’ credit transfer processes.

Research from the Government Accountability Office found that students who transfer lose an average of 43 percent of the credits they’ve already earned. But starting in July, accreditors must ensure that colleges provide a written explanation to students for every credit they deny and that those decisions are made before the student makes a “nonrefundable financial commitment.” Students must also be given an opportunity to appeal.

These new rules are a watered-down version of an earlier proposal that would have required colleges to effectively accept credit transfers by default, and they were only codified last week.

But it appears colleges have been preparing for the changes for months. At least one AI-powered credit transfer–evaluation platform has seen a spike in interest from institutions since Trump’s regulations emerged, and a number of state systems have been building pathways and establishing reciprocity agreements between their member colleges and universities.

And while Pruitt said efforts to improve the credit-transfer process—especially those led by public institutions—long precede the federal rule’s introduction in April, he noted that Trump’s attempt to crack down on the inefficiencies “certainly didn’t hurt.”

“By and large, our institutions knew that credit transfer had been an issue, and they needed an initiative out there to get it started,” Pruitt said. But the looming regulations were also a tool he used to encourage institutions to participate in the consortium. “I said, ‘Look, this is an opportunity for you to show the feds and everybody else that credit transfer is an issue we, as a higher ed community, are going to find a way to take care of.”

Scott Filter, director of government relations at the American Association of Collegiate Registrars and Admissions Officers, also stressed that while there are some technical concerns about the administrative burden of implementing Trump’s new rule, the industry was generally advancing in the same direction well before the proposal became public.

In February, the group released a report on best practices for improving credit transfer. And in September, it announced a campaign encouraging institutions to assume credits apply until proven otherwise.

The first report was shared with the department heading into the rule-making process, and “we think that it helped refine their conversations around transfer issues, since there wasn’t really a transfer expert at the table,” Filter said.

So, while the new regulations largely reinforce the need for work already underway, he said, for some institutions—particularly private colleges—it may be motivation to move faster.

“As they see those final regs coming into place,” Filter explained, “the institutions that aren’t at the forefront will probably realize that that is an important step they need to take.”

A Platform to Improve Access

Drew Melendres, co-founder of DegreeSight, a digital software application designed to facilitate a smooth and timely credit-transfer process for students and institutions, said that since the Department of Education first floated new rules about credit transfer in the spring, his phone “rings off the hook every day.”

“These regulations are driving many institutions to go, ‘How are we going to deal with this?’ And I think the word is out that DegreeSight already has a platform to do that, and we are seeing more interest in what we do now more than ever,” Melendres said.

The platform’s goal is to streamline the credit-transfer process for both students and administrators behind the scenes. When a student uploads a copy of their transcript, DegreeSight can promptly show them what credits an institution will take—as well as how close they would be to completing their desired degree. And if a course on the transcript hasn’t been evaluated for equivalency in the past, the software pulls data from other universities’ course catalogs to make equivalency recommendations and help faculty members and academic advisers make evidence-based decisions on whether to accept it.

More than 60 colleges and all institutions in the University of Georgia System were already using DegreeSight. Then, in late September, the National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics, which represents another 250 small colleges and universities, announced that it would also consider DegreeSight its “official credit evaluation platform.”

The partnership does not mean that all 250 institutions have automatically paid for DegreeSight’s services, but it does give them access to a significant discount, and Melendres anticipates that a number will take advantage of it. Eventually, if enough NAIA institutions sign up, there could be a more “standardized model” that makes transfers between any college in the association more efficient and helps ensure athletes, especially those who don’t go on to become pros, can transfer teams without losing progress toward their degree.

Unlike the CCU’s Transfer Credit Consortium, DegreeSight is not directly focused on getting institutions to collaborate and standardize their underlying policies on course equivalency. But he hopes that by providing colleges “as much data and information as humanly possible,” he can encourage them to broaden the number and types of credits they accept.

Having founded the company after serving as a vice president of enrollment management at two different institutions, Melendres has seen the inconsistent and arbitrary decisions that can be made when it comes to credit transfer.

He recalled a faculty member denying a student credit for the same course from a nearby community college he had already approved 39 times that same year. The reason? The faculty member knew the instructor who taught that student’s section and didn’t like him as much as he liked the other instructors.

Now, his goal is to stop that from happening, to provide more transparency for students and improve college access.

“I think that is exactly what the regulations are designed to stop from happening,” Melendres said. “And we are already equipped to deal with all of it, which is why our company is growing so fast. Institutions are calling us, knowing that this pending regulation is coming and they don’t have systems and tools in place, so we do help meet that need.”
