full_text:
When a young, untested former school teacher stood up to address a modest gathering of local donors in Austin, the state capital of Texas, Wendy Davis felt sorry for him. “Poor kid,” she remembers thinking.

Then James Talarico began speaking. “He was like five or six sentences in and I knew that something was different about him,” recalls Davis, a former Democratic state senator. “He was as articulate and unique then as he is now. From that day, I started calling him ‘Baby Obama’.”

Eight years after that first fundraising event, “Baby Obama” is no longer a precocious candidate for the state house with paper slogans that read “A future as bright as Texas”. Now 37, Talarico will aim to redraw the political map next week by becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the Lone Star state since 1988.

The threat that he poses to Republicans’ grip on power has become clear in the final stretch of a fraught campaign. Over the past month Donald Trump rallied in Texas and branded him “James Talafreako”; JD Vance implied that Talarico is gay (he has a girlfriend); and rightwing influencers spread a baseless lie that he checked into a mental health clinic in Ohio (he was ill with flu).

Despite the desperate attacks, most opinion polls give Talarico a narrow edge. On Tuesday the voters will have their say on whether the four-term state representative, a Presbyterian seminarian preaching a gospel of hope, can overcome Republican Ken Paxton, a scandal-haunted state attorney general and Trump ally who has financial backing from tech billionaire Elon Musk.

Facing a barrage of culture war attack ads funded by the world’s wealthiest man, Talarico has responded with an unorthodox blend of economic populism, progressive politics and an unapologetically Christian message that challenges the religious right on its own turf. His campaign raised a record $64m in the third quarter, including donations from a vast number of small-dollar contributors.

Last week Talarico told a crowd of young voters and local activists gathered at his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, that Republicans’ billionaire donors were starting to fret.“They are terrified because they see what we see: we are about to win this election,” he said.

An eighth-generation Texan, he was born James Dell Causey in Round Rock, a small town north of Austin, in 1989. His mother, Tamara Causey, was a preacher’s daughter who left home at 19 and met his biological father, whom she has described as an alcoholic prone to violence.

One night the abuse became too much. Tamara drove James and all her belongings in a small Ford Escort to the hotel where she worked as a sales assistant. They lived in an empty room at the hotel until they found an apartment in Austin. Tamara subsequently married a sales manager named Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname.

At school, Talarico was a keen debater and actor, with roles including Danny Zuko in the musical Grease. Allegra Hobbs, author of a profile in Texas Monthly magazine, reported: “His high school theater director, Aaron Johnson, joked to me that the young Talarico did not so much inhabit the character as play a version of himself. When the theater department handed out superlatives, ‘Jimmy’ was voted most likely to be president – a running joke among his friends that he would laugh off.”

Talarico studied at the University of Texas at Austin, where Mike Garcia, a 38-year-old lawyer and former legislative staffer, first encountered his political ambitions. In 2009, Garcia presided over the College Republicans while Talarico led the University Democrats. Despite their ideological differences, the pair initially found common ground in nonpartisan voter drives and a campaign for tuition relief.

Speaking from Fort Worth, Garcia recalls: “It was a little strange but I was glad that we were putting our differences aside and doing something that would help everybody.”

The goodwill did not last. During student government elections, Talarico’s organisation endorsed establishment candidates who opposed tuition re-regulation, according to Garcia. The move provoked outrage among Democrats who had supported the campaign, some of whom turned up at a College Republicans meeting to protest.

Garcia suspected Talarico had calculated that the endorsement would win him favour with university administrators ahead of a possible run for student body president. “That sounds like exactly something Jimmy would do,” he says.

Years later, when the two crossed paths again at the Texas capitol – Garcia working for Republican legislators and Talarico now an elected representative – Garcia felt he saw a similar gap between political rhetoric and personal charm. Talarico would “routinely just rail against all these people I work for, calling us the worst names ever”, he recalls, before greeting him warmly in the corridor minutes later.

Garcia remains unconvinced by Talarico’s current presentation as a moderate. “He is probably one of the types that is willing to tell you exactly what you want to hear, especially if it helps him politically. Right now he’s running as a moderate and he’s doing a very good job of it,” Garcia says.

But others dispute Garcia’s account. In a statement provided by Talarico’s campaign, Muneezeh Kabir, who was at the University of Texas with him and involved in student government, said: “James has always raised his hand to serve others. Throughout his time in student government at UT, James worked with everyone, even those he disagreed with, to make life on campus better for all of us. He delivered for his classmates at UT, then his community in Austin, and now, he’s ready to step up and serve Texans from every corner of the state.”

After college, and before the state house, Talarico went into education. His first job was teaching sixth-grade language arts at the Rhodes middle school on the west side of San Antonio, a predominantly Latino neighbourhood.

Edward Garcia, 56, who was principal of Rhodes at the time, remembers hiring Talarico during the summer of 2011. In a high-poverty school district where teacher turnover was relentless, Garcia was struck by the young applicant’s poise and purpose. “He knew what his mission statement was in terms of working with students that are in high poverty and high need. He was ready to start the next day,” he says.

Even before the academic year began, Talarico turned up at the school accompanied by his sister, hauling enlarged prints of Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr and Gandhi to create a classroom display devoted to human freedom.

“Teachers are supposed to be universal,” Garcia explains. “There wasn’t an approach in terms of partisan politics. It was just the concept of freedom and what it means for students to truly acquire freedom and leadership in their lives.”

Talarico’s connection with his middle schoolers was immediate. In a profession where novice teachers frequently struggle with classroom management and rely on administrative referrals, Talarico never wrote up a single student or sent one to the principal’s office. “He was an exemplary teacher. Kids were enthralled with his presentation and took a shine to him,” Garcia says. “What you see is what you get: smart, articulate and guided by his heart.”

When Garcia walked into Talarico’s room during his second-year formal observation, he discovered that the young teacher had physically removed his official administrative desk from the room.

“I went in to do his evaluation,” Garcia recalls with a laugh. “I looked around and said, ‘Where’s your desk?’ He goes, ‘Oh, I took it out and turned it into a reading space.’ He put a carpet down right where his desk should be.”

After two years in San Antonio, Talarico returned to the Austin area to lead an education non-profit before making his leap into elective politics in 2018. Winning a state house of representatives seat in a suburban swing district, he quickly established a reputation in the Texas capitol as an authority on public school finance and an exceptionally persuasive orator.

His Republican colleagues in the house began calling him “Baby Gov”, recognising that his ambitions might extend well beyond the state legislature. Talarico focused heavily on public education, prescription drug pricing and property tax relief.

During bitter legislative battles over voting rights and school vouchers – proposals to restrict access to the ballot and use public funds to help families pay for private education – Talarico emerged as a prominent opponent of Republican priorities.

In 2021, he joined fellow Democrats in leaving Texas to block a vote on Republican-backed voting restrictions by denying the state house the minimum number of members needed to conduct business. He later returned to the chamber before the standoff had ended, drawing criticism from some of his own party.

He also repeatedly clashed with conservative committee chairs over LGBTQ+ rights. Talarico used the phrase “God is non-binary” while opposing a bill concerning transgender children in school sports. Republicans have sought to weaponise it against him. Talarico has defended the underlying theological argument while acknowledging that he was being provocative.

While serving in the state legislature, Talarico enrolled at the Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, which has a picturesque downtown campus of neat lawns, light-filled buildings and functional classrooms with blackboards and rows of desks. He pursued a master of arts in theological studies, diving into church history, ethics, systematic theology and ancient biblical languages.

The seminary’s president, José Irizarry, says: “We are not an assembly line for dogma. We are a place of faith formation which requires people to think deeply and thoughtfully about their faith practices. What does it mean to take your belief system and actually do the work of justice in the world?”

Irizarry recalls working in his office across from the classroom building during Talarico’s first year. “I had no door when I arrived here – an actual open-door policy. He was studying Hebrew across the hall. I could hear the whole Hebrew class because it was with a rabbi and he started the class singing in Hebrew. I would go out during the breaks and see him interacting with all the students. He was a student like everybody else around here, engaged in ministry.”

When Talarico called Wendy Davis in late 2023 to disclose his intention to surrender his safe house seat and launch a long-shot bid for the US Senate, she tried to stop him. Davis, now executive director of the the Blueprint Texas political action committee, admits: “I tried hard to talk him out of it. I told him that my fear was he’d been so impactful in the legislature and I thought it would be a big loss for him. I told him he was probably going to lose and he was going to regret leaving his office. And now look at him.”

Talarico went on to defeat Jasmine Crockett, another rising star of the party, in a bruising Senate primary election. He has since been working hard to unify the Democratic coalition, including Black voters who supported Crockett.

His theological training has proven not merely a personal spiritual exercise but the construction of a political armour. In a state where conservative evangelicals have long dominated public discourse on religion, Talarico’s fluid command of scripture has allowed him to carry out a counteroffensive.

He attacks Christian nationalism, opposes state-mandated displays of the Ten Commandments in public schools and argues that Jesus’s core commandment – to love one’s neighbour – demands support for healthcare, public education and marginalised communities.

Cal Jillson, a professor of political science at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, says by phone: “Usually the vote that takes religion seriously in Texas is an evangelical conservative Republican vote. There’s a possibility that he has a little more purchase beyond the Democratic base into moderates and independent voters in the middle. With Talarico, there’s more of a Sermon on the Mount vibe as opposed to this ‘I’m an angry God’.”

Talarico demonstrated that approach during a legislative committee hearing on a bill requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in Texas classrooms. Rather than offering a standard secular objection, Talarico quizzed the author on the text of the Commandments themselves – showing on camera that the politician could not recite them.

For Democrats, there have been plenty of false dawns in Texas. In 2018 Beto O’Rourke’s charismatic campaign for Senate against Republican Ted Cruz attracted national attention and record-breaking fundraising, but he ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points.

Bill Minutaglio, a prominent Texas author and political historian whose books include A Single Star and Bloody Knuckles, argues that Talarico’s campaign represents a far more calculated and controlled evolution of Texas Democratic strategy.

“Beto was deemed to be the chosen one who would break the spell and obviously it didn’t happen,” Minutaglio observes. “He was a victim of inflated expectations. He seemed too ambitious and too coated with endorsements that didn’t resonate well outside the borders of Texas. People here don’t take kindly to the sense that a candidate is being shaped and endorsed by places like California or New York.”

Talarico, Minutaglio contends, studied O’Rourke’s missteps to avoid repeating them. “O’Rourke appeared on the cover of Vanity Fair magazine. Talarico has learned his lessons. I don’t mistake his quietude and his seminarian step for him not being a truly shrewd politician. He is that and then some. The ability to walk that fine line is rather amazing to me. I find it almost Obama-like. There’s a calmness about him and a thoughtfulness in public. He’s playing right now five-dimensional chess in Texas,” he says.

Part of that strategy involved building a political identity of his personal narrative and Christian faith. “It’s become that sense of armour – holding up the Bible – and people can’t get around it,” Minutaglio says. “Paxton, of course, is the greatest foil that anybody could pray to have. Talarico has found the cheat code in Texas.”

The contrast between the two candidates could hardly be starker. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted overwhelmingly to impeach Paxton on 20 articles alleging misconduct, including bribery, abuse of office and obstruction of justice. The state senate later acquitted him.

A long-running state securities fraud case ended in 2024 with an agreement requiring Paxton to perform community service, pay restitution and complete legal ethics courses in exchange for prosecutors dropping the charges. Paxton has remained bogged down by public revelations regarding his personal life, including an alleged extramarital affair and a high-profile divorce.

Paxton, 63, has also been lethargic on the campaign trail with even Trump poking fun at his dress sense and speaking style. Jon Taylor, a professor of political science at the University of Texas at San Antonio, says: “Paxton is afraid to meet people. He tries to stay in this shell and avoid voters.

“Everywhere Talarico goes, he attracts a substantial crowd. He’s got rock star status. Talarico is charismatic, personable and tells stories that resonate. Meanwhile, his opponent is basically screaming that Talarico believes God is non-binary and that he’s ‘far left’. The message is viewed by voters as shrill and ineffective.”

As the race entered its final lap, national Republicans realised that Paxton’s vulnerability risked forfeiting a seat crucial to maintaining their narrow Senate majority. In response, conservative Super Pacs launched an unprecedented financial bombardment.

Musk, who moved Tesla, SpaceX and his personal residence to Texas, gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The Republican Super Pac subsequently transferred the money to the Texas Pac, which has blanketed the state’s 22 media markets with anti-Talarico advertising. The blitz focused almost entirely on trans culture-war themes, falsely claiming Talarico supported taxpayer-funded gender reassignment surgeries for minors.

At the same time, cracks have emerged in the conservative coalition along the Texas-Mexico border. While Trump made significant inroads among Latino voters in 2024, recent aggressive immigration raids and agricultural disruptions appear to have produced widespread buyer’s remorse.

Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, a political consultant and former Democratic US Senate candidate, says: “I always say that the portion of Latino voters up for grabs are neither Republicans nor Democrats – they’re poor, and they need candidates who speak to their poverty, their pain and their power.

“Talarico leans more on a moral calling than a political persuasion, and that vision connects to people across a much larger swath of political persuasions than Democrats historically have reached. People are sick of the brazen political corruption and the system not working for ordinary working people.”

Democrats are taking nothing for granted in a state that Trump won by 14 percentage points against Kamala Harris in 2024. Talarico is still careful to characterise himself and his movement as the people-powered underdog against the oligarchy, the David taking on a Goliath that includes the world’s most powerful man and the world’s richest man. For supporters who have spent decades enduring Democratic defeats in Texas, the prospect of a Talarico victory feels less like an ordinary midterm result than a profound turning point.

Minutaglio comments: “If Talarico wins, it will be huge – a sea change in modern Texas history. The reverberation will rocket from the Fortune 500 companies in Dallas to the oil barons in Houston and the high-tech moguls around Austin. For decades, Texas has been addicted to deregulation and unfettered capitalism. Here’s a quiet seminarian who says, ‘Pump the brakes. Let’s think about oversight.’ It will challenge every perception of what Texas is.”

full_text:
It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parents and professors, and their dealings with a common antagonist: the university.

The first character we meet is Sri Lankan teen Devi, who is set on obtaining offers from “Ochpys” – her acronym for Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale and Stanford. To help her realise her dream, Devi’s family of modest means – her mother, father, maternal grandmother and two brothers – hire themselves out as mourners at the funerals of the wealthy. Most of this money goes towards paying Johannes, her tutor on WhatsApp who, unbeknown to Devi, is a hard-up Indian student at Arcadia Tech, an undistinguished university in the US. Meanwhile, Jack, a statistician at the same institution, has taken on an additional teaching load to meet the fees of the elite college his daughter Katrina attends in New England. Soon he catches on to a grade-fixing scheme aimed at flailing international students, run by his teaching assistant Allard Hamburger. Jack is left in disbelief when, to buy his silence, the university puts him on paid administrative leave instead of launching an inquiry into a scandal that has left one student dead by suicide.

Boyagoda keeps the narrative charged with drama through an ever-evolving gallery of characters and their never-ending problems: yet-to-be-Dr Allard, who suffers from daddy issues and intends to endow a research chair at the Ivy League school where his long-absent father Martin teaches astronomy; his all-but-PhD mother Patricia, who had been teaching research methods to undergraduates until she was replaced by a chatbot named Puck; Katrina and her roommate Cham, a Sri Lankan refugee raised in Rome. The best of friends from the moment they met and shared their stories – Cham’s separation from her family and adoption by the Sri Lankan ambassador; Katrina’s mother laid low by breast cancer – the two are now quietly feuding. This is partly because they are unwelcome on university premises, thanks to Cham, whose idea it was that they sabotage a protest version of the 14th-century romance Sir Gawain and the Green Knight in a bid to be radical on their own terms. By sticking to the original script instead of observing a sit-in like the rest of the cast, they have partaken in a play that “perpetuates speciesist, sexist, racist, ableist, ageist and Christianist ideologies that are also deployed in support of settler-colonial Zionist apartheid fascist regimes”.

A campus novel of the present moment, Lords of Serendipity is animated by the upheavals reshaping American universities and the wider world: the pressures put on higher education by the Trump administration, the steady erosion of the humanities, Israel’s devastation of Gaza, as well as the threat of AI and the fact that “everything with substance and history, with texture and nuance, with seriousness, gravitas, was being replaced with flatness and shine and more flatness and shine”. Boyagoda has no end of things to say about “the corruption upon corruption upon corruption of the university”, its growing subordination to corporate interests, what is lost in that process, and how for many students from the global south a western education may not be “a lifestyle thing, or an experience” but an expensive pathway to immigration.

Part of what makes this book propulsive as well as engaging and thought-provoking beyond its topical significance is Boyagoda’s voice, which is intellectually agile without being self-congratulatory, and incisive without squandering its whimsy and impishness. Boyagoda, who is a professor of English at the University of Toronto, has both good and bad jokes, and he often wields them at his own expense, poking fun at everything from the interpretive excesses of English literature scholars to the proclivity of humanities folks to cast themselves as the “eternal torture victims of the university”.

Many things happen in this novel – too many to describe here. The most unexpected development concerns the Chinese takeover of a university in the Sri Lankan city of Kurunegala, which is renamed Serendipity in a grim and ironic evocation of the island’s colonial past (“Serendib,” we are told, “was the original name of Sri Lanka itself, when Europeans and Chinese explorers first found it and were so unexpectedly happy and amazed by their discovery”). The university becomes the new base for Martin’s work on colliding stars, after he abruptly loses his research chair at his home institution. Jack, who has been persuaded to join this new venture, will find himself once again at the centre of a scandal that puts his integrity to the test.

Meanwhile, after barely pulling through a series of dispiriting setbacks, Devi approaches Jack in the hope of turning her luck around. That we live in an unequal but interconnected world is hardly a revelation; in this tragicomic tale, full of crooks and strivers, opportunists, dreamers and mercurial patrons, Boyagoda’s genius lies in humanising this entanglement, and revealing its contradictions.

title: With students scarce, college admissions offices get friendlier, less intimidating
summary: Colleges are trying to transform an admissions process that has often been daunting, secretive and stressful into an experience that's open, easier — and downright friendly.
full_text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

SARATOGA SPRINGS, N.Y. — Overwhelming.

That's how 17-year-old high school senior Alex Zaret described the college admissions process, during a tour of the Skidmore College campus — the fourth school Zaret had visited, with another half-dozen to go.

"It is kind of a full-time job," Zaret's father, Owen, said.

He wasn't joking. With research to do, visits to make and applications and financial forms to fill out, "it's a lot, and it's a lot on top of two full-time-employed parents and a very engaged high school student," Owen Zaret said.

But even in the year or so that the family has been doing this, the Zarets have detected a subtle shift.

At first, the process seemed to be what Owen Zaret called an ivory tower approach. It signaled: "'You're lucky if you come here.' And now, I think, for a variety of reasons, that's changed. It's more like, 'We want you to be here.'"

Hurting for students, colleges are striving to transform an admissions process that has often been intimidating, secretive and stressful into an experience that's open, easier and downright friendly.

"It's one of those things that's in everybody's interest," said Marc Conner, president of Skidmore, which has been making a particular push to do this. Even though application and enrollment data show his college is not among the many others having trouble filling seats, he said, "We depend on students coming to our campuses and, when they do come, getting them to enroll."

Some universities and colleges are waiving application fees and promising additional financial aid for students who show up for campus tours. Public universities in 17 states now admit high school students who haven't even applied, according to the Education Commission of the States; more than 150 private colleges also make direct admissions offers to students who fill out the Common App, a standardized online application used by about 1,200 institutions. And the overall odds of getting accepted to college are going up.

Now Skidmore and a small number of other institutions have taken a surprising next step: enlisting faculty to help recruit new students — a role they previously left entirely to the admissions office — by meeting with and opening their labs and classrooms to prospective and admitted applicants.

"It creates a feeling of what it would be like to be seen, valued and to find a place of belonging on a campus," said Jess Ricker, the college's vice president for enrollment. And that, Ricker said, can help distinguish Skidmore from the other schools on students' lists.

Admissions leaders are looking for any advantage. Two-thirds of them had trouble meeting their enrollment targets in at least one of the last two years, according to a survey by the ratings platform Niche. Ninety-seven percent expect the competition to increase.

The reality they face: The supply of traditional-age freshmen nationwide is projected to decline by 13 percent over the next 15 years, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. The proportion of high school graduates choosing to go on to college is also down, from 70% in 2016 to 63% in 2024, the most recent year for which the figure is available, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports.

Good news for students, not colleges

One little-noticed result: Being accepted to college is generally easier than it has been in the past and than Americans seem to think it is.

Nearly 8 in 10 first-year applicants for undergraduate admission to public and 7 in 10 to private colleges and universities get in, the National Association for College Admission Counseling, or NACAC, reports. That's up from 68% and 65%, respectively, about 10 years ago. Nearly 9 in 10 private, nonprofit four-year universities and colleges admit half or more of applicants, according to separate research by the conservative think tank the American Enterprise Institute.

This news has been slow to trickle down to students. More than 40% of 18- to 29-year-olds wrongly think it's harder to get into college than it was for people in their parents' generation, a Pew Research Center survey found.

"Most of the public actually doesn't understand that the majority of institutions in the United States actually accept the majority of students who apply," said Angel Pérez, NACAC's CEO.

He blamed an obsession with acceptance rates at institutions such as CalTech, Harvard, Princeton and Stanford, which each take about 1 applicant in 25.

In fact, only 33 colleges and universities in the country admit 10% or fewer of their undergraduate applicants, NACAC figures show.

The intensifying competition for them might be good for students, but it's bad for many colleges. At some, offices of admission are struggling to shake what Ricker joked is their historic reputation as "offices of rejection."

A few, including Skidmore, are appealing to the faculty for help. At Ohio Northern University, at least one member of the faculty now meets with every visiting applicant. Faculty at Washington College in Maryland sit down with visiting applicants on designated Fridays during the admissions season and at open houses.

"Presidents and vice presidents of enrollment are telling people that every interaction counts." said Rob Springall, a consultant at the executive search firm WittKieffer and former executive director of undergraduate admissions at Pennsylvania State University.

There's another reason for this that's less widely understood among consumers. As students hedge their bets by applying to more colleges than their historical counterparts — Common App users now apply to an average of more than seven schools apiece, a number that's been steadily increasing — it's getting harder for enrollment managers to predict how many they admit will actually enroll. In admissions lingo, this is called the yield.

Yield has declined from 32% in 2014 to 22% in 2024 at public and from 24% in 2014 to 18% in 2024 at private, nonprofit colleges and universities, on average, federal data shows. That's the last period for which the figures are available.

This means colleges have to admit around five times as many students as they need — and that admitted applicants need to be persuaded to follow through and put down their deposits, including the many of them who come back to take another look around.

Reluctant faculty get in on the recruiting

Colleges "are realizing that everyone has to help with the recruiting process," said Leah Beth Hubbard, assistant vice president of enrollment strategies at the enrollment consulting firm The Parish Group. She advises clients to "teach everyone to smile. Teach everyone to introduce themselves and say what they do at the institution."

Coaxing faculty to do this, on top of their existing obligations, isn't always easy, campus leaders said — at least, at first.

"Some faculty didn't want to be part of it," said Johnnie Johnson, Washington College's vice president for enrollment management. "They'd say, 'You go recruit and I'll teach.'"

Like other university and college administrators, Johnson said he countered with a frank assessment of enrollment trends.

"When you put a financial figure on every student who comes in, that equates to programmatic funding. That equates to raises," he said. And faculty are seeing what happens when those numbers fall. "They have colleagues who have been at colleges that closed" or whose programs have been cut, said Johnson. "They don't want to be next."

Skidmore, which has 2,719 students, hasn't experienced the problems many other small private, nonprofit colleges are confronting. It's seen its number of applications rise, not fall; unlike colleges in general, its acceptance rate is down, from 37% 10 years ago to 24% today. Yield is an above-average 24%.

Still, said Conner, the president: "Even if the school is doing all right during these times, we're still facing the same headwinds as everybody else."

Everyone from dining hall workers to groundskeepers are encouraged to be welcoming, he said.

"It helps that we're in a tough time in higher ed and they see what's happening at other schools," said Conner. "And they know a school is going to rise or fall depending on how much the community joins together."

More than three-quarters of admitted students who came to the campus last year other than for a weekend open house requested to sit in on a class or meet with a faculty member, the college says. That added up to 300 personal visits.

There's not yet data about whether those young visitors apply or enroll. But Psychology Department Chair Becca Johnson, who often meets with applicants, said she hears feedback that it makes a difference.

One mother told her, " 'You know, my student has applied to so many schools, been accepted, had a number of wonderful possible possibilities,' " Johnson recounted. " 'And you're the first person from outside of an admissions office to contact us. And that was so meaningful for them in their decision."

This story was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education.

title: Inside the AP's process for calling election races
summary: Millions of votes have been cast in this midterm election. Traditional battlegrounds have expanded in the fight to control Congress. It all comes down to one question: who won? This year, PBS News is again relying on the Associated Press to call winners in critical races. For a closer look at how the AP makes those race calls, Deema Zein spoke with David Scott of the Associated Press.
full_text:
Amna Nawaz:

The 2026 campaign has been the most expensive in U.S. history, and it's all leading to tomorrow night, when the votes are counted.

Deema Zein has a look at what happens next.

Deema Zein:

Millions of votes have been cast in this midterm election. Traditional battlegrounds have expanded in the fight to control Congress. It all comes down to one question: Who won?

This year, the "News Hour" is once again relying on the Associated Press to call winners in critical races.

For a closer look at how the AP makes those race calls, I'm joined by David Scott, V.P. of election services at the Associated Press.

David, thanks for joining us.

David Scott:

Happy to be here.

Deema Zein:

So I want to jump right in. People watching results on election night want to know the winner. So tell us, how do you know when the race is over and which candidate won?

David Scott:

So the thing that we're looking at primarily is the vote count. We are reflecting the choices that Americans have made at the ballot box as they make their choice about who they want to lead the country, who they want to represent them in Congress or in the statehouse.

And so we start there. And, really, the question we're asking ourselves is, are the trailing candidates or a trailing candidate able to catch the leader?

And when we have determined, based on all of the evidence, primarily the vote count, but other things that we take into account, what happened in the advance vote, what's the history of a state, what our poll shows about what took place and what voters were thinking about on election night, but really the vote count, when we see and we are certain that the trailing candidate can't catch up, that's when we declare a winner.

Deema Zein:

And who makes that ultimate decision?

David Scott:

We have got a big team at the Associated Press that makes up our decision team. And they're all journalists. They are people who cover politics. They are data analysts. They are experts in political science.

They are folks who study this year-round full-time. We have folks who focused on turnout and what the expected vote it is. What's the denominator? How many votes are going to be cast in this election? And then, of course, the numerator, what are each candidate getting?

And, again, we're trying to answer that question. When we look at all the votes that have been counted so far, what do we see about what's outstanding? And has a candidate reach the point where none of the others are able to catch them and they will be the winner? And that's when we declare a winner.

Deema Zein:

And not until that moment.

David Scott:

Not until that moment. Our certainty is our standard. We're not trying to be first. We're not trying to race to a decision. We are looking at what's coming in. But we also feel an obligation to let an the voters know, to let America know, this is who you have chosen to lead.

And so we're being swift, but always focused on accuracy first. Our standard is certainty. We are certain when we declare a winner that the trailing candidates can't catch up.

Deema Zein:

Do bad calls actually happen? And, basically, why should Americans trust AP to get it right?

David Scott:

We have been doing this literally since the founding of the Associated Press; 1848 was the first time that we counted the vote and declared winners two years after the founding of a cooperative. It's part of who we are as a news organization.

We think that the choices that Americans have made is a news story. It's really important. In this year's primaries, we declared winners in more than 11,000 races. And we made three mistakes. And one was because of bad information from election officials, for example. And another one was because of a technical problem. So they do happen, but they're very rare.

Deema Zein:

David Scott, vice president of election services at Associated Press, thank you so much.

David Scott:

Happy to be here.

title: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
summary: Democratic gains in Congress could bring tougher oversight of major companies and shift billions of dollars in federal spending and regulatory policy.
full_text:
watch now

Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue. Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency.

For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage.

A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies, challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation.

Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes.

Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat.

"We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore, head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley.

For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense, healthcare, banking and artificial intelligence.

"There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist at LPL Financial.

Congressional oversight and investigations

Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings.

Companies are already getting a preview.

On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook, as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors.

While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras.

"It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra, Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes.

Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital, and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency.

Andrew Harnik | Getty Images

Federal spending

Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes.

Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill, is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments.

Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion, or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.

A Democratic-controlled chamber could not repeal the 2025 law on its own but could use must-pass budget negotiations to seek funding changes or delays to some cuts.

"They're probably going to push back on those Medicaid cuts," Buchbinder told CNBC, noting that preserving coverage could help stabilize enrollment for Medicaid insurers and patient volumes for hospitals.

Hospitals face their own squeeze: fewer insured patients can mean more uncompensated care, while state budget pressure can reduce reimbursement rates, according to KFF. Congress created a $50 billion rural health fund over five years to cushion some of the blow, but KFF and medical providers have said the money would not fully offset the broader Medicaid reductions.

Democratic gains could still cut both ways for healthcare. The same lawmakers seeking to protect Medicaid funding could also intensify scrutiny of insurers, hospitals and drugmakers over prices, coverage and profits.

Khanh Vu | Reuters

Defense contractors face a fight over which weapons and programs Congress keeps funding. The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, with a focus on replenishing weapons, bolstering readiness and covering other needs, some tied to the Iran war.

The White House is separately seeking an $87.6 billion supplemental appropriation from Congress for fiscal 2026, driven primarily by military operations related to Iran.

A Democratic Congress could challenge some Iran- and Israel-related spending while pushing for more aid to Ukraine. However, bipartisan consensus on China deterrence, nuclear modernization and missile defense could protect other major programs, according to multiple analysts.

For contractors, the difference could mean billions of dollars in orders.

Lockheed Martin, for example, recently reached a framework agreement with the Pentagon covering 850 F-35 fighter jets over a decade. But the agreement is not yet a finalized contract: Congress must authorize the multiyear purchase and provide the funding.

"You want to be a stock picker and not just ride the whole sector," Guerra told CNBC, pointing to areas such as shipbuilding, autonomous systems and missile defense as likely winners.

Daniel Cole | Reuters

Rules and regulations

For crypto companies, the midterms could determine whether Trump's regulatory shift becomes durable law or remains vulnerable to the next administration. The industry's push for permanence stalled in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Trump-backed Clarity Act, a sweeping market structure bill.

Shares of Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as 11% when the measure failed.

Getting a bill through the next Congress could come at a price. Democratic gains would give the party more leverage to demand stricter consumer safeguards, limits on yield-bearing stablecoins and tighter scrutiny of Trump's crypto businesses.

"In some ways, the industry doesn't really care who got elected," said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. "They just want to know what the rules are going to be for the coming year."

Banks are looking for durability, too.

Federal regulators estimate their proposed capital overhaul would cut requirements for the largest banks by roughly 4.8%, potentially freeing billions for lending and shareholder payouts. The Federal Reserve writes the rules, but Senate control shapes who fills future vacancies, and congressional committees can pressure regulators through hearings and investigations.

"It's at the regulatory level where stuff can happen that matters," Buchbinder said.

Stephanie Keith | Getty Images

AI may be the messiest political trade of all.

Trump has made rapid data center construction an economic and national security priority. Morgan Stanley expects hyperscalers including Microsoft , Amazon , Alphabet and Meta to spend more than $1 trillion on capital projects in 2027, even as the buildout faces growing backlash over electricity bills, water use and infrastructure costs.

CNBC's All-America Economic Survey from October found that 63% of registered voters oppose having a data center within 10 miles of their home, compared with just 13% who support one. The level of opposition is higher from Democrats than Republicans.

That friction has already reached Congress. In September, the House voted 417-3 to require state regulators to consider making large data centers cover the additional electricity infrastructure costs needed to serve them. The measure stalled in the Senate, 57-43 on a procedural vote, after Democrats argued it was too weak and pushed for mandatory protections instead of trusting the industry to police itself.

The midterms therefore could decide who gets the power. Democratic gains could put more grid-upgrade costs on tech developers, raising project costs just as access to power is constraining new construction.

But Congress is only part of the equation. State regulators, utilities and local governments will still decide where projects connect to the grid and which facilities get built.

"We think the election can have meaningful consequences, but on a highly localized basis," Salvatore said.

title: New Zealand student experience hits record high, but work opportunities lag
summary:
International student satisfaction in New Zealand has reached its highest level since national surveying began, though students continue to report difficulties finding work alongside their studies.

The post New Zealand student experience hits record high, but work opportunities lag appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Nine in 10 international students rated their overall experience positively in the 2026 New Zealand International Student Experience Survey, released by Education New Zealand (ENZ), up from 87% in 2025.

Almost half (47%) described their experience as “excellent”, with both measures reaching their highest levels since the survey began in 2019.

“Students have delivered a pretty clear verdict. They value the education they receive here, however, just as importantly they value the experience of living here and the connections they make with people,” said ENZ chief executive David Downs.

“That matters. International education isn’t only about getting students to New Zealand. It’s about making sure they have a great experience on the journey here, and that experience continues once they arrive.”

The survey heard from 6,129 international students representing more than 100 nationalities, with education and living experiences both recording their highest scores since the survey began.

Some 91% of students rated their education experience positively, while 90% were positive about their living experience. According to ENZ, living experience had the strongest influence on students’ overall satisfaction, followed by education.

People and connections was the highest-rated area, at 93%, while arrival and orientation reached a record 92%. Some 93% of respondents described their teachers, supervisors and tutors as supportive and respectful, and 91% rated New Zealand positively as a safe place to live.

But Downs said the findings also highlighted practical challenges facing international students.

“A good survey shouldn’t only tell you what you want to hear. Students are also being very clear about the practical things that can make their experience harder, particularly finding work, managing costs and accessing some support services,” he said.

Work experience remained the lowest-rated of the seven aspects measured, with 55% of students rating it positively – unchanged from 2025.

Just 33% were positive about the ease of finding part-time work during their studies, amid a challenging employment market affecting domestic and international students and graduates alike.

“Work experience is the standout challenge,” said Downs.

“We need to keep strengthening the links between study, employers, and career opportunities so students can see a clear pathway from a great education to strong career outcomes.”

Cost pressures also remain an issue, despite perceptions of value for money improving to a survey high of 78%. Students were less positive about the costs associated with living, education and international travel.

As more students choose New Zealand, protecting what they value and acting on the areas where they say we can do better will be critical to sustainable growth

David Downs, Education New Zealand

The findings come as New Zealand looks to grow its international education sector while maintaining the student experience that underpins its appeal as a study destination.

The government’s International Education Going for Growth plan, announced in 2025, set out an ambition to increase international enrolments by 35,000 and nearly double the sector’s value to NZ $7.2 billion by 2034. Measures including increased student work hours and expanded post-study opportunities signalled the country’s return to growth, with an emphasis on quality and sustainability.

“Growth and student experience have to go together,” said Downs.

“As more students choose New Zealand, protecting what they value and acting on the areas where they say we can do better will be critical to sustainable growth.”

International education export earnings have already reached NZ $4.98bn, surpassing the sector’s pre-pandemic value of NZ$4.403bn in the year to June 2019.

Student numbers, however, remain below their pre-pandemic peak. New Zealand recorded 92,580 international student enrolments in 2025, compared with 115,705 in 2019, while the country is on track for around 99,000 enrolments in 2026.

title: What Sets Florida’s Elite Colleges Apart
summary: Campus Region This index of Florida universities and colleges features research universities and undergraduate-focused colleges, with schools listed first according to their research strengths and then their overall breadth and strength. Some schools that are specialists in particular fields have also been given credit for having a strong and well-developed program in their area of […]
full_text:
This index of Florida universities and colleges features research universities and undergraduate-focused colleges, with schools listed first according to their research strengths and then their overall breadth and strength.

Some schools that are specialists in particular fields have also been given credit for having a strong and well-developed program in their area of specialization. This is not a ranking based on acceptance rates, but you’ll find that the schools that appear on this list vary widely in their reputations and selectivity.

Here are some of the best colleges in Florida for challenging students: From developing an original project during a summer at Stetson to studying animation at Ringling to finding a research group at a large public university, there are many different paths to a challenging Florida college experience.

Each of the schools profiled below has particular strengths, and our goal in selecting them was to show you the range of options and discuss in practical terms the differences among degree programs, faculty advising and mentoring, and opportunities for meaningful work while in college. (For instance, our profile of Embry-Riddle focuses on its Daytona Beach campus.) We hope that our discussions of what makes these schools special will help you learn more about these colleges and figure out which might be the right fit for you.

15

Jacksonville University

Builds Experiential Learning Into Undergraduate Study

Experiential learning isn’t limited to just one department; it’s part of the student experience at Jacksonville University, which is a private university with a close-knit campus community and a riverfront location.1

Jacksonville University’s academics page notes that the university’s Experiential Learning program expects students to participate in an experiential learning activity, such as research, study abroad, service or internship.2 Those are four very different options, so the degree programs clearly don’t all expect students to participate in all four.

Jacksonville’s academics page makes a distinction between undergraduate programs, graduate programs, and combined programs.

That helps, especially for a school that offers several learning options. Prospective students can look through Jacksonville University’s programs to figure out which ones might suit them.

Some students are interested in internships so that they can try out a career, while others might want to participate in research to explore a question that interests them. The value of experiential learning opportunities depends on the quality of the work students are expected to do, the amount of guidance they receive, and how the experience connects to their degree. But for students who are looking for an education with more to offer than just a professor standing up front of the classroom talking, Jacksonville University can give them some practical skills to walk out the door with after graduation.

14

Florida Southern College

Supports Faculty-Guided Undergraduate Research

Florida Southern College is a small liberal arts college, not a large research university.

And yet Florida Southern’s small size provides a setting for rigorous undergraduate research. Florida Southern’s undergraduate research program is just one aspect of the academic offerings at the College.

However, research opportunities are strengthened by Florida Southern’s other academic resources, ranging from degree programs and support services to the Honors College.3

Together, these resources provide a holistic system for undergraduate education that goes beyond promising to foster critical thinking and instead offers students concrete opportunities to hone this skill. Of course, research looks different in different academic disciplines.

At Florida Southern, some forms of research may mean carefully following a scientific protocol in a lab, while others may emphasize the rigor required to create a work of art. Nonetheless, from the information currently available, Florida Southern’s commitment to undergraduate research is clear. Students work alongside faculty mentors to pursue projects of their own design from as early as their first year of college.4

They learn to formulate research questions, focus overly broad topics, find evidence to support their claims, and adapt their research plans as necessary, building research skills.

And, though they work under faculty supervision, students contribute to projects, which makes Florida Southern’s research opportunities particularly worthwhile.

13

Stetson University

Structures Independent Research Through a Summer Program

Stetson’s Undergraduate Research Experience (SURE) is an eight-week summer research program in which students work closely with a faculty member on an individual research or creative project.5

It’s competitive, as students apply and are selected university-wide, but if you’re selected, you’re in for a rewarding summer of research, working one-on-one with a faculty mentor on an original project. And, the research doesn’t end there.

SURE Scholars present their research at the Stetson Showcase and often at other professional conferences.6

The research experience is just as important as the research presentation, since learning to explain your research question, methodology, and findings to an outside audience is a challenge in itself. Stetson offers the opportunity, though finding a research mentor and developing a viable research proposal is up to you.

Applying does not guarantee an award.

12

Eckerd College

Connects Liberal Arts Study With Its Waterfront Setting

Studying the environment near your doorstep can be uniquely interesting because it’s familiar to you, but at Eckerd College it can also mean participating in a research project with faculty and fellow students.

In St. Petersburg, Eckerd College is more than adjacent to the water, as the institution uses its waterfront location as a teaching and research site. Rather than simply serving as a pretty backdrop, Eckerd’s natural surroundings offer opportunities for research projects and internships, experiences that even first-year students can participate in.7

Other experiences that complement coursework and a major of study at Eckerd include: First-Year Research Associateships, an Honors Program, a research symposium, and a Senior Capstone project.8

Research and other experiences offered through coursework provide an ongoing educational experience. While the experiences mentioned above take place on Eckerd’s St. Petersburg campus, the college also offers internships and global educational experiences.

With such robust research, internship and global experiences paired with mentorship from faculty members, it’s easy to see how a liberal arts and sciences education at Eckerd College differs from that of other private colleges and universities. Before applying to Eckerd College, think about what you’d like to study there and how your experiences will evolve during your time as an Eckerdian.

11

New College of Florida

Pairs Semester Contracts With a Senior Capstone

All students follow a core curriculum,9 but they also engage in independent research and pursue highly individualized programs of study.

Students do not simply pick courses from a catalog; instead they work with an adviser to develop a semester contract. Together they negotiate a challenging course of study that might include Independent Study Projects, tutorials, laboratories, and other individually designed activities.

Advisers offer detailed written comments on student work.

For both adviser and advisee, the semester contract poses interesting challenges: What courses or projects work well together? What does progress look like during the term?

The culmination of an individualized New College education is a senior capstone or thesis defended in a final examination.10 It may take the form of a documentary film, artistic project, or traditional research paper. The goal is to carry an idea through to completion, and then be prepared to discuss and defend that work.

We suggest that you take a look at the current curriculum.

Understanding the relationship between a core curriculum and individualized learning isn’t an afterthought; it is at the heart of a New College education.

10

Ringling College of Art and Design

Builds Creative Study Around Student Projects

For people interested in getting an education in art and design, Ringling College of Art and Design may be a suitable school.

Finished work speaks louder than any course description. And Ringling College of Art and Design makes this easy by showing off work from students in each of its programs.

For example, in the 3D Character Animation program, animation, visual development, and story development are all treated as part of one cohesive discipline.11

It’s an area of study that rewards iteration and practice, because excelling at one aspect of character animation (timing, character, visuals, story) can prompt rethinking in others. It’s that kind of intellectual rigor, wrapped up in an environment where making and critiquing creative work are at the center, that makes Ringling stand out.

The college offers a host of programs beyond just this specialism, with plenty of majors, minors, and certificates.12

9

Rollins College

Introduces Liberal Arts Study Through Discussion

Rollins College ranks ninth in our list thanks to its emphasis on critical thinking through discussion-based learning.

Rollins College is a liberal arts college located in Winter Park.13 Rollins College is known for its interdisciplinary Rollins Foundations in the Liberal Arts curriculum that allows students to explore subjects outside of their intended major and take general education courses in an interdisciplinary fashion.

In order to develop strong critical thinking skills, Rollins College has a required discussion-based seminar class called the Rollins College Conference for all entering students.14

In this class, students learn more about the people who will support them during their time at Rollins and meet fellow students who are also just starting out. Students are expected to come prepared, offer their own insights and interpretations, listen to the ideas of others, and reevaluate their positions as necessary.

This allows students to form habits of mind that can be applied in any subject. Students benefit from having a similar starting academic experience, which can also help them as they decide on a major and navigate degree options. If you’re interested in attending a smaller school with close relationships with faculty and meaningful discussions, this may be the right fit for you.

8

Florida Institute of Technology

Connects a Scientific Tradition With Several Fields

Florida Institute of Technology is well known for its science and technology programs, but that’s hardly all it offers.

The university offers programs in business, aeronautics, psychology and the liberal arts as well,16 and its graduate programs (which extend to the doctoral level) also delve into a host of fields. Originally known as the Brevard Engineering College, the university was founded in 1958 by then-Cape Canaveral employee (and physicist) Jerome Keuper.15

Florida Tech encourages its students to think in terms of more than one discipline, for example, why stop with sound design when you can also learn about user behavior?

Why limit yourself to instrumentation when you could also be interpreting data? The school’s focus on research means that Florida Tech students can expect plenty of hands-on experience both in the field and in the lab, and that’s true for undergrads as well as those working on master’s degrees and beyond.

That is not all, as Florida Tech’s programs are interdisciplinary by nature, giving students exposure to several related areas of expertise at once. That’s an important skill, since most problems call for a variety of solutions. Florida Tech’s intimate connection with the Space Coast lends an element of context to the university’s impressive history and technological focus, but its wide range of academic programs and undergraduate opportunities should ultimately play a larger role in your decision to attend.

7

Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach

Combines Aviation With Business, Science, and Engineering

While aviation shapes Embry-Riddle’s identity, Embry-Riddle offers degrees in arts and sciences, aviation, business, and engineering at its four colleges.17

Flying, designing systems, and managing companies are very different things, and require different kinds of preparation and skills. Embry-Riddle’s four colleges reflect this breadth.

In the full degree directory you’ll find Embry-Riddle degrees in aviation, engineering, business, security, and the sciences.18

Not all of these degrees are offered at each level and on each campus, though, so be sure to take note of that as you explore. Interested in learning more about careers in aviation or space?

With so many different degrees, it’s important to do your research and find the one that best aligns with your interests and career goals. You might love flying, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that you should go into aviation without considering all of your options.

6

Florida International University

Offers Research and Flexible Subject Combinations

Ranked sixth on our list for its research efforts and the interdisciplinary connections it fosters, Miami’s public research university19 has a lot to offer students interested in crafting a unique path through higher education.

At Florida International University, majors can be paired with a choice of minors or certificate programs to create a personalized degree plan. A biology major, for example, might want to add an entrepreneurship minor,20 while a student who studies digital communications may want to earn an artificial intelligence certificate.

FIU’s interdisciplinary credentials combine technical know-how with an understanding of how ideas find their way into the hands of end users.

FIU is a leader in research in fields such as computing, public health and engineering. Its research addresses varied challenges, and students are encouraged to explore as many areas of study as possible.

Collaboration among colleges at FIU leads to innovative interdisciplinary credentials. With so many options available, it’s important to make sure that the path you chart will be manageable and won’t have you bogged down in red tape. Check out the degree plan requirements at FIU and learn how to maximize your time there.

5

University of Central Florida

Offers Broad Programs Across Central Florida

Founded in 1963 to develop engineers for the nation’s space program,21 UCF has since expanded.

Now UCF offers programs in a downtown hub, a hospitality setting, health sciences centers, traditional settings, and through online and distance learning.22 The best way to learn about “what is a UCF degree” is to explore all the settings in which UCF offers its programs, ranging from laptop to lab coat, and there’s likely to be a UCF for you.

When thinking about your best college fit, consider practical matters like where you’ll take classes, what resources will be available to you, and even what format your classes will take, since these details may be even more important than a school’s size.

4

University of South Florida

Pairs a Research University With Small Honors Classes

Not all students will benefit equally from USF’s research accomplishments.

The university’s membership in the prestigious Association of American Universities23 and the breadth of USF Health research, patient care, and education in Tampa Bay do not necessarily mean that you, as an undergraduate, will be exposed to research in your major. For motivated students, the Judy Genshaft Honors College provides small classes and close interaction with faculty,24 which you won’t find in big lecture halls.

Honors students also benefit from academic support services, study spaces, and living-and-learning communities that ease the adjustment to college.

The honors college is just one route for students to take advantage of USF’s resources, but it does have special requirements. As you consider USF, be sure to take into account opportunities available to students in your major, as well as in the research environment and in smaller communities like these.

When you can see a university’s accomplishments and feel the connection they have to you, that’s when its prestige has real meaning.

3

University of Miami

Structures Advanced Research Within Academic Departments

The University of Miami is composed of several schools (architecture, communication, engineering, arts and sciences, and music just to name a few),25 which can influence a student’s undergraduate research experience .

To get a sense of the breadth and depth of research Miami offers its students, it helps to look at a department. Miami’s biology department offers an Honors program which includes a minimum two-semester original research project under the supervision of a faculty member.

The student is expected to present and defend his or her project publicly and will also produce a written thesis.26

Miami’s biology department suggests students contact specific faculty or the Office of Undergraduate Research for information on finding a mentor. However, the specifics of Miami’s Honors program in biology aren’t necessarily representative of Miami as a whole.

Still, it’s useful as an example of the sort of things applicants should look for in other departments and disciplines. What are the sequential steps in doing research at Miami? What is the relationship between student and faculty mentor?

How is student work used?

Projects that evolve over multiple iterations of questions, evidence, and revision can simulate a more authentic scholarly environment. Looking at how research unfolds in one department can provide valuable insight into how research at Miami can contribute to an applicant’s undergraduate experience.

2

Florida State University

Connects Early Research With Discussion and Presentation

There are a variety of ways to get involved in research as an undergraduate at Florida State.

Ranked number two for visible paths into original scholarship, Florida State doesn’t just encourage undergraduate research, it lays out some pretty clear options for how to get started. First- and second-year students (including transfers) can get involved in the University Honors Program, which offers small Honors courses and additional academic support to encourage students to begin their research careers as early as possible.

Students who are further along in their academic careers can still perform original research with the assistance of a faculty member through the Honors in the Major program.27

FSU also offers the Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program (UROP), a research assistantship for first- and second-year students. Students in UROP participate in a discussion-based course and can research across disciplines (not just lab-based science!).

At the end of the program, students present their research at the Undergraduate Research Symposium.28 Not only will participation in UROP familiarize you with the research process. You may meet other students doing research in your field that may spark even more ideas.

And presenting your research will give you practice talking about your work with an audience.

Whether through the University Honors Program or other opportunities at FSU, eligibility varies by program.

1

University of Florida

Combines Academic Breadth With Research Support

Our top pick is the University of Florida because of its extensive array of programs and research options for undergrads.

UF offers degrees at the undergraduate, graduate, and professional levels.29 The UF Honors program provides research advice and points students to research opportunities in their areas of interest.

The Center for Undergraduate Research, departmental opportunities, and University Scholars can also help students find faculty mentors and research opportunities.30

The University of Florida offers many ways for students to gain research experience, but each option has specific requirements. Students should keep this in mind when deciding to pursue research at UF.

As with any research opportunity, students should be prepared, seek the right mentor, and be willing to commit the time and effort to research projects, which are often undefined at the outset. For these reasons, as important as access is, we also valued support in our assessment. UF is the top school on our list thanks to this blend of research support and breadth of programming.

That said, don’t attend UF just because it’s UF.

Consider what you hope to gain from attending UF and whether it’s the right school for you. If you can find the right major, come up with a cost-effective plan for attending, and find research opportunities that align with your interests, UF might be a suitable school.

title: heise+ | Herausforderung Legacy-Modernisierung: Strategien für die Zukunft
summary: Der Artikel beleuchtet Strategien zur Modernisierung von Legacy-Systemen, analysiert Entscheidungskriterien sowie Risiken und zeigt Lösungsansätze auf.
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

Legacy-Softwaresysteme sind seit Jahrzehnten fester Bestandteil vieler Unternehmen, Behörden und Organisationen – und das aus gutem Grund. Sie haben sich in geschäftskritischen Bereichen bewährt, bieten Stabilität, Zuverlässigkeit und hohe Performance, unterstützt durch moderne Hardware, die selbst KI-Anwendungen ermöglicht. Diese Systeme sind ausgereift, was ihre weiterhin hohe Verbreitung erklärt. Doch trotz dieser Vorzüge stellt die fortschreitende Digitalisierung Unternehmen vor eine komplexe Herausforderung: Wie lassen sich bewährte Lösungen mit zukunftsfähigen Innovationen vereinen?

Kompakt

Legacy-Systeme sind stabil und zuverlässig, aber schwer mit modernen Innovationen vereinbar.

Ihre Modernisierung birgt Risiken wie Systemausfälle und Compliance-Probleme, da sie geschäftskritisches Wissen enthalten.

Eine erfolgreiche Legacy-Modernisierung erfordert strategische, technische und organisatorische Ansätze.

Obwohl der Modernisierungsbedarf oft offensichtlich ist, werden entsprechende Projekte häufig nur zögerlich angegangen oder sogar zurückgestellt. Die Gründe dafür sind vielfältig: Das Risiko einer Migration ist enorm – ein Ausfall der Systeme könnte Millionenverluste oder regulatorische Probleme bedeuten. Hinzu kommen die extreme Komplexität und der hohe Kostenaufwand, da diese Systeme jahrzehntelang angesammeltes Geschäftswissen in Code enthalten. Sonderfälle, Ausnahmen und historisch gewachsene Regeln zu extrahieren und neu zu implementieren, ist eine gigantische Aufgabe. Der Mangel an Fachkräften für Legacy-Technologien und das klassische „Never touch a running system“-Prinzip verstärken diese Herausforderung zusätzlich.

IT Spektrum 6/26

In diesem Beitrag beleuchten wir, wie Unternehmen diese gewaltige Aufgabe systematisch angehen können. Wir betrachten verschiedene Aspekte der Legacy-Modernisierung, von der strategischen Planung über technische Lösungsansätze bis hin zu Best Practices, um eine erfolgreiche Transformation zu gewährleisten. Eine kluge Balance zwischen bewährten Systemen und innovativen Ansätzen kann die Zukunftsfähigkeit von Unternehmen langfristig sichern.

Das war die Leseprobe unseres heise-Plus-Artikels "Herausforderung Legacy-Modernisierung: Strategien für die Zukunft". Mit einem heise-Plus-Abo können Sie den ganzen Artikel lesen.
